item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Trump-Xi Summit Opens as Treasury Yields Hit 19-Year High
item.description: Trump and Xi meet at the White House as Treasury yields spike to levels unseen since 2007, pushing mortgage rates past seven percent. Plus, a judge restores press access at the White House, and an AI pricing war breaks out between Anthropic and OpenAI.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, September 24th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump and Xi Jinping are sitting down at the White House this morning for their biggest meeting in years, and it's happening while Treasury yields are sitting at their highest level since 2007.

ANDREW: And overnight, a federal judge ordered the White House to restore press credentials it stripped from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW last week. We'll get into what that ruling actually does, and doesn't, settle.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,706, down about eight tenths of a percent. The Dow fell seven tenths of a percent to 51,511. The Nasdaq dropped just over one percent to 26,936. It was a rough session across the board, and the reason is the bond market. The ten-year Treasury yield jumped to roughly 5.1 percent yesterday, a level we haven't seen since 2007. The thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking near 7.2 percent according to Mortgage News Daily. We'll dig into what's behind that move in a few minutes.

ANDREW: Let's start with the story of the day. Presidents Trump and Xi are at the White House this morning for a summit that's supposed to touch almost everything at once.

JENNY: What's actually on the table?

ANDREW: The headline item is trade. The two sides agreed to extend their tariff truce by another two months, which avoids a fresh economic shock but doesn't resolve the underlying disputes. Taiwan is on the agenda, so is the war in Iran, and so is artificial intelligence. The one concrete piece that seems likely to come out of today is a formal notification channel the two governments would use to warn each other about AI incidents that touch on national security. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China's Vice Premier He Lifeng agreed to that in principle over the weekend, after roughly eight hours of talks in New York, and today is really about whether that turns into something both sides actually sign.

JENNY: Is anyone expecting an actual breakthrough, or is this more about just not making things worse?

ANDREW: Mostly the latter. Foreign policy analysts going in were clear that avoiding a new escalation between the world's two largest economies would itself count as a win. Nobody is predicting a resolution on Taiwan or a lasting trade deal out of one meeting, and Trump himself signaled as much this week.

JENNY: What did he say?

ANDREW: At the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump described a broader deal, one that also touches Iran, as nearing, without offering specifics. That's the tone going into today, incremental progress dressed up as a summit rather than a single dramatic announcement.

ANDREW: Sticking with Washington, that press credentials story. A judge named Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that the White House likely violated the due process rights of CNN, Politico, and MS NOW when it revoked their reporters' permanent access passes last Saturday without notice or a hearing. He granted a fourteen-day temporary restraining order requiring the administration to restore access immediately.

JENNY: So is this over, or does the fight keep going?

ANDREW: It keeps going. Kelly's order is temporary, not a final ruling, and the underlying case continues. But it's a meaningful early setback for the administration. Kelly wrote that the standard the White House offered for pulling the credentials was so vague, in his words, it hardly does the trick. It's also worth noting Kelly is the same judge who ordered CNN's Jim Acosta reinstated back in 2018, so the White House was arguing in front of someone with direct experience on exactly this question.

ANDREW: One more to track here. The Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed, with something like one commercial transit a day against a normal baseline near ninety. A senior Iranian official said this week Tehran could reopen it within about a week if Washington eases military pressure and unfreezes Iranian assets, a real softening from where things stood even last week. Whether today's summit produces any movement there is probably the biggest swing factor for oil prices heading into the weekend.

ANDREW: Now let's get into what's actually happening with rates, because the bond market move we mentioned up top is really the story underneath everything else this morning.

JENNY: Walk me through it. Why are yields spiking now?

ANDREW: Two things stacked on top of each other. The Fed already raised its benchmark rate a quarter point back on September 16th, its first hike in three years, and signaled it's not done, with most officials penciling in at least one more increase before year end. Then this week, a batch of stronger than expected business activity data raised fears the Fed might have to move even faster. Longer-term yields react to expectations, not just the last decision, and that combination pushed the ten-year up to levels we haven't touched since 2007.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for somebody trying to close on a house this week?

ANDREW: It's not good news. Mortgage News Daily has the top-tier thirty-year fixed rate at roughly 7.26 percent as of yesterday, up sharply from about 7.17 percent just two days earlier, and matching the highs we saw back in early 2025. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, which runs a little cooler because it averages the whole week, had the thirty-year at 6.95 percent last Thursday, itself up from 6.76 percent the week before. Both are pointing the same direction, and Freddie Mac's fresh weekly number is due out today.

JENNY: Is the Fed actually done hiking, or should people expect this to keep going?

ANDREW: The Fed's own projections say no, they're not done. Sixteen of the eighteen policymakers who submit forecasts penciled in at least one more quarter-point hike before the year is out. So until that changes, the pressure on mortgage rates is more likely to persist than ease.

ANDREW: Demand is already responding. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey, for the week ending September 18th, showed total application volume down one and a half percent, with refinancing activity down three percent and now sitting sixty-two percent below where it was a year ago. Purchase applications slipped about one percent, and within that mix, adjustable-rate loans ticked up to nearly ten percent of all applications, a sign some buyers are trying to dodge the fixed-rate spike altogether. None of that is a collapse, but it's a market cooling in real time as rates climb.

ANDREW: Jenny, your beat is next. What's happening in AI?

JENNY: A genuine price war broke out this week. Anthropic released Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, pricing it at four dollars per million input tokens and twenty dollars per million output tokens, close to its flagship model's performance at a lower cost. Within hours, OpenAI answered with two new models, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, undercutting Anthropic by half on price.

ANDREW: What does a price war like that actually mean for a bank or a big enterprise buying these tools?

JENNY: It's a meaningful shift in leverage. Enterprise customers who were locked into paying premium prices for frontier-level performance are suddenly getting that same tier of capability for a fraction of the cost, which should accelerate adoption in places like financial services that had been more cautious about the expense. The flip side is that both companies are racing on price just days after their own CEOs stood up at the United Nations and called for a slowdown in AI development.

JENNY: That UN moment actually connects back to what Andrew mentioned earlier. The AI notification channel that's expected to come out of today's Trump-Xi summit builds on the same safety conversation Sam Altman and Dario Amodei were pushing at the Security Council this week, where China's DeepSeek and Moonshot were in the room alongside the American labs for the first time. That inclusion alone was notable, it's the first time Chinese labs have been part of that kind of formal safety briefing at the UN.

JENNY: One more thread we've been following: OpenAI and Anthropic have reportedly been close to a legally binding deal to stress-test each other's models, something they first did informally last year, when OpenAI probed Claude's safety behavior and Anthropic ran OpenAI's models through its own misalignment testing. As of this week, that follow-up agreement still hasn't been finalized, even as the two companies keep racing each other on price and capability.

JENNY: Let's shift local. Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near 84 today, mostly cloudy and breezy with a good chance of afternoon showers and thunderstorms. The National Weather Service also has a coastal flood advisory in effect starting this evening through Friday morning, so plan around some standing water if you're near the river or the beaches.

JENNY: JEA's leadership transition hits a real marker tomorrow. CEO Vickie Cavey's resignation officially takes effect Friday, and the board is holding a special meeting that same day to lay out next steps on finding her permanent replacement.

ANDREW: Any sense of who's in the running, or is this just about setting up the process?

JENNY: Right now it's about the process. Interim CEO Jody Brooks stays in place while the board works that out, and Friday's meeting is expected to focus on the search timeline rather than any actual candidates.

JENNY: And locally, the Jacksonville Civic Council, a group of about ninety business and civic leaders, came out this week against Amendment 3, the statewide ballot measure that would raise Florida's homestead exemption to 150,000 dollars in 2027 and 250,000 dollars the year after. According to city council auditors, that would cost Jacksonville's city government at least 300 million dollars in lost revenue within two years, and the Civic Council warns it could slow police and fire response times and make it harder to recruit officers and firefighters.

ANDREW: That's a striking number against a city budget that council just finished trimming.

JENNY: It is, and that timing isn't a coincidence. That two billion dollar city budget passed eighteen to one this week partly because council found room to restore an affordable housing fund that had been on the chopping block. A revenue hit of that size would land right on top of those same tight-margin decisions next time around.

JENNY: One last local item to flag: the JTA's overhaul of the downtown Skyway is still on track for a decision in October. Six alternatives remain on the table, ranging from about 150 million dollars for a basic modernization up to 565 million dollars for a full streetcar conversion, and public input sessions continue over the next couple of weeks before the board weighs in.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch: the Trump-Xi summit runs through Friday, and the real test is whether it moves past vague agreements into anything concrete. Watch specifically for two things, whether that AI notification channel gets formally signed rather than just agreed to in principle, and whether there's any signal tied to Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days. A real move on Hormuz is probably the single biggest catalyst for where oil prices, and by extension those Treasury yields and mortgage rates we talked about this morning, go next. Keep an eye on Brent crude too, it's been climbing for days on the uncertainty alone.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Iran Signals on Hormuz, AI's First UN Briefing, Jax Budget Passes
item.description: Iran hints the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within days, a day before Trump meets Xi. Sam Altman and Dario Amodei brief the UN Security Council on AI for the first time. Jacksonville's budget passes with housing funds restored.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Wednesday, September twenty third. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: A senior Iranian official says Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if Washington eases its pressure campaign, a real shift in tone one day before Trump and Xi Jinping sit down in Washington.

ANDREW: And on the other side of the world, Sam Altman and Dario Amodei briefed the UN Security Council on AI safety together for the first time ever. We'll get into what that actually accomplished.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed essentially flat Tuesday, around seven thousand seven hundred sixty five. The Dow slipped about one hundred eighty five points, or four tenths of a percent, to just under fifty one thousand nine hundred. The Nasdaq was the outlier, up about a half percent to a fresh record close near twenty seven thousand two hundred fifty, powered again by chip and AI stocks. The ten year Treasury yield sits just under five percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking right around seven percent, according to Mortgage News Daily. Falling oil prices helped sentiment Tuesday, tied to some cautious optimism out of the Middle East, which is exactly where we're headed first.

ANDREW: Let's start with Iran, because the posture actually changed overnight.

ANDREW: For weeks, Iran's position on the Strait of Hormuz has been rigid. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf kept saying Tehran wouldn't reopen it or return to talks until the US met a list of conditions. That held right through last week. But a senior Iranian official now says the strait could reopen within seven days if the US eases its military pressure, lifts the naval blockade on Iranian ports, and releases frozen Iranian assets.

JENNY: So what changed? Why now?

ANDREW: Timing is everything. This comes one day before Trump sits down with Xi Jinping in Washington, a meeting tied to this week's UN General Assembly, where Iran is expected to be squarely on the agenda alongside trade and Taiwan. Trump himself said at the UN Tuesday that a deal is, in his words, nearing. For context, the strait is a chokepoint for roughly a fifth of the world's oil, and shipping through it is still down to a trickle, about one transit a day compared to nearly ninety before the crisis. So it's still closed right now. This is a signal, not a resolution.

JENNY: Worth watching what comes out of that meeting tomorrow, then. Is there any read on how the White House itself is framing this?

ANDREW: Publicly, optimistic but noncommittal. Trump's team wants to avoid promising a breakthrough and then not delivering one, especially with oil markets and mortgage rates both sensitive to how this resolves. If Hormuz genuinely reopens, that's downward pressure on oil prices and, by extension, on the Treasury yields that drive mortgage rates. If it doesn't, expect the tension to carry right into the weekend.

JENNY: So this one touches almost every other story on the show today.

ANDREW: It does, which is exactly why we're leading with it. We'll flag it again at the end of the show.

ANDREW: Separately, Trump signed a security agreement with Denmark and Greenland's leaders Tuesday at the UN, formalizing something that had been expected for about a week. It gives the US expanded, effectively permanent military basing rights on the island. Denmark and Greenland keep sovereignty, but the US gets what amounts to a veto over any other country, meaning China or Russia, getting access to bases, troops, or sensitive investment there. It's essentially an updated version of a nineteen fifty one basing pact between Greenland and NATO, just with much broader terms. Parliamentary ratification in Denmark and Greenland still has to happen before it formally takes effect, but the signing itself is done, closing out a story we've been tracking for about a week.

ANDREW: One more to flag, a story we've been following closely: the press freedom lawsuit. CNN, Politico, and MS NOW sued the White House after their reporters lost credentials. The Justice Department filed its response Tuesday night, arguing that White House access is a privilege, not a right, and pushing back hard against restoring it. Judge Timothy Kelly, who ruled for CNN in a nearly identical case back in twenty eighteen, holds a hearing on this at three thirty this afternoon. We don't have an outcome yet, that's this afternoon's news.

JENNY: We'll know by tomorrow's show, at least.

ANDREW: We will. Jenny, speaking of firsts, your beat had one too.

JENNY: It did. The UN Security Council held its first ever briefing dedicated to frontier AI safety Tuesday, and it was a genuinely unusual lineup.

JENNY: Sam Altman briefed in person, Dario Amodei joined by video, and they were joined by AI researcher Yoshua Bengio and Hugging Face's Clement Delangue. But here's the detail that matters most. China's DeepSeek and Moonshot were also invited to speak, sitting alongside their American rivals. That's the first time the Council has put Chinese and US frontier labs in the same session.

ANDREW: Did anything concrete come out of it, or was this mostly symbolic?

JENNY: Mostly symbolic for now. Altman pushed for international benchmarks to actually measure AI capabilities and safeguards, instead of every lab grading its own homework. Nothing binding got adopted. But getting Beijing's leading labs and Washington's leading labs into the same UN session, even just for a briefing, is new. It fits with something else happening this week: Treasury Secretary Bessent and China's Vice Premier agreed in principle over the weekend to set up an AI incident notification channel between the two countries, with a follow up meeting in Shenzhen in about two months. Still not binding, but it's the same direction.

JENNY: And that UN session came on the same day as something a lot more commercial. Anthropic and OpenAI both cut prices Tuesday, hours apart.

ANDREW: Wait, on purpose, the same day?

JENNY: Looks that way. Anthropic released a new model, Opus five point five, roughly forty percent cheaper than its predecessor while matching higher end performance. OpenAI answered with two new models of its own, priced roughly half of what their prior generation cost. It reads like a price war for enterprise customers who are sensitive to the cost of running AI at scale, which is a little ironic given both CEOs have publicly called for the industry to slow down.

ANDREW: Nothing says slow down like a same day price cut.

JENNY: One more data point on that same theme. Recent industry surveys put financial services near the top of every sector ranking on AI adoption, second only to the tech industry itself, with a large share of firms now calling their AI use advanced rather than experimental. The most common use case isn't a flashy chatbot, it's mundane stuff, like closing the books faster at the end of the month.

ANDREW: That tracks with what we're seeing in mortgage lending too, honestly. The back office is where a lot of this actually shows up first.

JENNY: It is. Let's bring it back home. Jacksonville is looking at a high near eighty five today, a mix of sun and clouds with a real chance of pop up afternoon storms. Winds pick up out of the northeast, gusting near twenty five miles an hour, so keep an eye on the sky if you've got outdoor plans.

JENNY: The big local story: city council passed Jacksonville's budget Tuesday night, eighteen to one.

ANDREW: Didn't we say yesterday that affordable housing amendment was still up in the air?

JENNY: It was, right up until the vote. Councilman Matt Carlucci's floor amendment to restore the four point nine million dollars cut from the affordable housing trust fund passed twelve to seven, with a modification from Councilman Ron Salem that splits the money. About two million goes to down payment assistance, roughly a million and a half toward the capital stack, and the rest toward utility tap fees for attainable housing projects. City staff had estimated that money could help six to seven hundred households.

ANDREW: So the cut got reversed in the end.

JENNY: It did. The only no vote on the full budget was Councilman Rory Diamond.

JENNY: Also worth flagging, the Jaguars' stadium renovation hit a milestone. The city issued its largest permit yet on the project earlier this month, valued at just over half a billion dollars. Team president Mark Lamping says it's about fifteen percent complete and on schedule, with more than five hundred workers on site daily and the canopy truss steelwork wrapping up by November. Capacity will be reduced to around forty two thousand five hundred for this season while the work continues.

JENNY: Downtown, there's real momentum too. The Gateway Jax project is advancing five sites near Pearl Square, the old Ambassador Hotel is being converted into a new Marriott property called the Hotel Merrydelle, and the city issued a permit for a rebuild of the Jacksonville Shipyards marina. None of these are massive standalone headlines, but taken together, it's some of the most downtown construction activity we've tracked in months.

JENNY: Two more to watch by the end of the week. JEA's board meets Thursday, the same day CEO Vickie Cavey's resignation officially takes effect, which should be our first real signal on how the utility handles finding a permanent replacement. And JTA is still working through six options for the aging Skyway system, ranging from about one hundred fifty million dollars to reuse it, up to five hundred sixty five million for a full streetcar conversion. A preferred option is still expected in October.

JENNY: Andrew, over to you for home lending.

ANDREW: Rates actually eased a little this week. Mortgage News Daily had the thirty year fixed at seven point one seven percent Tuesday, its best level in about a week, and a separate survey from Fortune had it even lower, just above seven percent Wednesday morning. The ten year Treasury yield, which mortgage rates track closely, has drifted down toward four point nine six percent, partly on those Iran de-escalation headlines we opened with.

JENNY: So is this the start of a real drop, or just noise?

ANDREW: Cautiously, just a pullback, not a trend yet. Rates are still solidly above seven percent by most measures, and the industry isn't betting on a big move down. The Mortgage Bankers Association actually just trimmed its own origination forecast for next year to just over two point one trillion dollars, citing an expectation that rates hold closer to seven percent for longer than hoped. Fannie Mae made a similar, smaller downward revision.

ANDREW: One more note. The MBA's weekly application data, which usually comes out Wednesday mornings, hadn't posted as of this taping. Worth checking back for that update, since the last reading showed applications down about four percent, with refinancing activity down sharply too.

ANDREW: And one small regulatory footnote. Federal regulators quietly bumped up next year's exemption threshold for higher priced mortgage loan appraisal rules, to just over thirty four thousand dollars, effective January first. Not a headline number, but it's the kind of technical adjustment that keeps the lending pipeline moving without much fanfare.

JENNY: A lot of threads to keep an eye on this week.

ANDREW: There are. Before we let you go, one thing to watch: tomorrow's meeting between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping in Washington. It's tied to this week's UN gathering, and the agenda is stacked, covering Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, trade and tariffs, Taiwan, and that AI notification channel Jenny mentioned. Watch specifically for any concrete movement on Hormuz shipping, that's the single biggest thing that could shift oil markets and interest rates together by the end of the week.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Wednesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Greenland Security Deal, Press Freedom Suit, Markets Hit Record Highs
item.description: The US and Denmark strike a landmark Greenland security deal, three networks sue the White House over a press ban, and Wall Street closes at a record. Plus cooling mortgage rates and AI rivals OpenAI and Anthropic edge toward testing each other's models.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Tuesday, September twenty second. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The United States and Denmark have reached a landmark agreement giving Washington a much bigger security role in Greenland, while three major news organizations are suing the White House over a ban on their reporters.

ANDREW: And Wall Street closed at a fresh record yesterday, with a rally in AI stocks pushing AMD past a trillion dollars in market value for the first time. We'll get into what that's doing to mortgage rates.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at roughly seven thousand seven hundred sixty five, up about one and a half percent. The Dow finished at fifty two thousand fifty, up about seven tenths of a percent. The Nasdaq closed at twenty seven thousand one hundred twenty two, up about two and a quarter percent, a fresh record and its first since back in June. Falling oil prices and easing Treasury yields drove the rally, along with another surge in AI-linked stocks. AMD crossed a trillion dollars in market value for the first time, its fifth straight day of gains, and Meta jumped more than eleven percent after its new AI assistant, Muse, topped the app store download charts. The ten-year Treasury yield eased to just under five percent, and the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking right around seven percent this morning, according to Mortgage News Daily.

ANDREW: Let's start in Washington, because the biggest development of the last few days might be getting lost in everything else going on. The United States and Denmark have reached a deal giving Washington what the administration is calling permanent security control over Greenland.

JENNY: Wait, control, does that mean the US actually owns it now?

ANDREW: No, and that distinction matters. Denmark and Greenland's governments are being explicit that no sovereignty is changing hands. What the US gets is an expanded military footprint and a much bigger security role, essentially an updated version of a nineteen fifty one pact between Greenland and NATO. The agreement also specifically locks out China and Russia, barring them from bases, troops, or sensitive investments on the island.

JENNY: This is the same Greenland Trump talked about taking by force at one point.

ANDREW: It is, which is what makes this notable. It's a negotiated outcome to a standoff that started with the president threatening to just take the territory. Denmark, Greenland, and the US are expected to formally sign it this week in New York, timed to the United Nations General Assembly, though Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers still need to ratify it before it actually takes effect.

JENNY: So still not fully done until that happens.

ANDREW: Right, the ink isn't dry yet. But all three parties agreeing to terms, without Denmark ceding sovereignty, is the story.

ANDREW: Meanwhile, three major news organizations are now suing the White House. CNN, Politico, and the network now called MS NOW, formerly MSNBC, filed suit Monday after the administration barred their reporters from the building and pulled their credentials.

JENNY: On what grounds did they get banned in the first place?

ANDREW: The White House hasn't laid out a detailed legal justification. The outlets say it's retaliation for coverage the president didn't like, and that's the due process argument at the center of the suit. It landed in front of Judge Timothy Kelly, a Trump appointee who, worth noting, ruled in a nearly identical case back in twenty eighteen, when CNN's Jim Acosta had his credentials pulled and got them back. Kelly ordered the Justice Department to respond today, with a hearing set for three thirty tomorrow afternoon.

JENNY: So we could know fairly quickly whether this holds up.

ANDREW: We could. If Kelly follows his own precedent, that's not a great sign for the administration's position.

ANDREW: One more to track, a story we've been following closely: Iran isn't budging on the Strait of Hormuz. Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said again this week that Tehran won't reopen the strait or return to talks until Washington meets a list of conditions, including releasing frozen assets and ending what Iran calls a blockade on its ports. If anything, the position has hardened since last week, not softened.

JENNY: And Thursday's summit between Trump and Xi Jinping is supposed to be where this gets some kind of push forward.

ANDREW: That's the hope in Washington. Analysts expect Iran to be on the agenda alongside trade and Taiwan, since China has leverage over Tehran that the US doesn't. Nothing guarantees a breakthrough, but it's the most direct venue either side has had in weeks.

ANDREW: One quick note on the Fed. Chair Kevin Warsh's tension with the White House hasn't escalated further the last couple of days, but it hasn't cooled off either, and Senate Republicans have been publicly defending the central bank's independence. That standoff is part of why the ten-year Treasury yield spent last week climbing toward levels we haven't seen since 2007, even though it eased back a bit yesterday along with everything else.

JENNY: So the Fed fight is still simmering under all of this.

ANDREW: It is. It's just not the loudest story right now, with everything else happening in Washington this week.

ANDREW: Jenny, over to you. What's happening in Jacksonville?

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near eighty seven today, humid, with a couple of morning showers and a good chance of thunderstorms again this afternoon.

JENNY: Tonight is the big one locally. City council takes its final vote on the new budget, and the fight over four point nine million dollars for the affordable housing trust fund comes to a head. As we've reported, the finance committee voted seven to one last week to strip that money out, with council president Nick Howland casting the deciding vote. Councilman Matt Carlucci is bringing a floor amendment tonight to put it back.

ANDREW: Does he have the votes this time?

JENNY: Still unclear. He's not asking colleagues to decide tonight exactly how the money gets spent, just to preserve it. City staff estimate that four point nine million could help somewhere between six hundred and seven hundred households, split between new construction, down payment assistance, and utility hookup help for low income residents. It comes down to who actually shows up to vote tonight.

ANDREW: We'll find out by this evening.

JENNY: In other local news, JEA's board is now set to meet this Thursday, September twenty fifth, the same day CEO Vickie Cavey's resignation officially takes effect. That's the first real marker for when we might hear a timeline on a permanent replacement. Interim CEO Jody Brooks stays in the role until then. And JTA's board still hasn't narrowed its six options for the aging Skyway system downtown, ranging from about one hundred fifty million dollars to modernize it to over five hundred million for a full streetcar conversion. That decision remains on track for October.

JENNY: One more from the Jaguars: defensive end B J Green is headed to injured reserve with an elbow injury and will be out about four weeks. The team elevated linebacker Jack Kiser to the active roster and signed B J Ojulari to the practice squad for depth, which the team will need after Sunday's loss in Denver.

JENNY: Andrew, how are mortgage rates looking after that stock rally?

ANDREW: A little better, actually. The thirty year fixed is hovering right around seven percent this morning, according to Mortgage News Daily and The Mortgage Reports, essentially flat to slightly lower than yesterday. That continues the pullback we've seen since last week's one year high near seven and a quarter percent. Zillow's broader survey, which averages differently, still shows something closer to seven and a quarter, so where you land depends on which lender or tracker you check, but the direction the last few days is down, not up.

JENNY: Is that connected to the stock market having such a good day?

ANDREW: Directly. Falling oil prices and easing Treasury yields are two sides of the same story, and mortgage rates track the ten-year yield closely. When yields ease the way they did yesterday, mortgage pricing usually follows within a day or two.

JENNY: So does that change anything for somebody trying to buy right now?

ANDREW: Not dramatically. We're still talking about rates well above where they sat a month ago. The real test comes tomorrow, when the Mortgage Bankers Association releases its weekly applications data for last week. Their last reading showed applications down four percent, with more buyers reaching for adjustable rate loans to manage the payment. Tomorrow's number tells us whether that pullback in demand is accelerating or stabilizing now that rates have eased a bit.

JENNY: We'll be watching that one. Anything on the regulatory side?

ANDREW: Quiet. No fresh moves from the CFPB or FHFA in the last day or two to flag.

ANDREW: Jenny, you've got some genuinely new AI news today.

JENNY: I do, and it's an unusual one. OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly negotiating a deal to let each other test their own models.

ANDREW: Wait, they're letting a competitor poke around inside their systems?

JENNY: Sort of. Multiple outlets are reporting the two labs are close to a legally binding agreement that would give each side API access to the other's already-released commercial models, specifically for independent safety stress testing, with a clause guaranteeing neither side keeps or trains on the other's data. It's not finalized, so call it a work in progress, but if it happens, it would be the first time two frontier labs formally agreed to test each other rather than just talk about safety in the abstract.

ANDREW: That's a real shift from a year of these companies mostly just racing each other.

JENNY: It is, and it builds on something else we've been tracking. Remember Anthropic's plan to embed outside evaluators inside its own operations, with the consulting firm Accenture? That's now confirmed by multiple outlets, not just the one newsletter we flagged last week. Accenture's Faculty AI unit will get employee level access to red team Anthropic's models, with both companies committing at least a billion dollars each over five years. Sam Altman said back on the twelfth that OpenAI would match that approach, though OpenAI still hasn't named its own version of Accenture yet.

JENNY: There's also a government to government piece tied to Thursday's summit. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and China's Vice Premier He Lifeng spent eight hours in New York over the weekend and came out of it agreeing in principle to set up a formal channel for flagging AI incidents that touch national security before they turn into bigger disputes between the two countries. A follow-up meeting is already scheduled in Shenzhen in about two months. It's not a signed treaty, more an agreement to build the plumbing for one, but that's further than these talks had gotten before.

ANDREW: Given everything else on the agenda Thursday, that's a lot resting on one meeting.

JENNY: It is. One more data point for context: a recent survey found seventy three percent of finance and insurance firms are now paying for AI tools, up from around sixty percent at the end of last year. Financial services is adopting this faster than almost any other sector.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Thursday's meeting between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping in Washington, tied to the UN General Assembly. Three separate threads converge there. Whether China uses its leverage to get any movement from Iran on reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Whether the Denmark-Greenland security agreement actually gets signed as planned. And whether that new US-China AI notification channel becomes something more concrete than a handshake. Watch for whether Thursday produces an actual outcome on any one of those, rather than just another round of talks.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Tuesday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Trump Escalates Supreme Court Attack, Iran Hardens Before Trump-Xi Summit
item.description: Trump blasts the Supreme Court as Iran hardens its Hormuz stance before Thursday's Trump-Xi summit. Plus: Treasury yields hit an 18-year high, Google discloses a Gemini red-team surprise, and Jacksonville's budget fight heads to Tuesday's vote.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning, and welcome back from the weekend. It's Monday, September 21st, 2026. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: President Trump spent the weekend attacking the Supreme Court directly, while Iran hardened its position on the Strait of Hormuz just days before Thursday's summit between Trump and China's Xi Jinping.

ANDREW: And the ten-year Treasury yield closed Friday at its highest level since 2007, which is already showing up in mortgage rates. We'll get into what that means for anyone house hunting right now.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed Friday at seven thousand six hundred fifty, up two tenths of a percent. The Dow finished at fifty one thousand six hundred eighty two, down about a tenth of a percent, its third straight losing week. The Nasdaq closed at twenty six thousand five hundred twenty two, up about four tenths of a percent. For the week, the Dow fell one point seven percent, its worst week since March, while the Nasdaq actually gained about seven tenths of a percent. The split screen there is the Fed's first rate hike in three years working through the bond market and Treasury yields climbing to multi-year highs. The ten-year yield closed Friday at just over five percent, its highest close since July of 2007. And the thirty year fixed mortgage rate is tracking around seven percent this morning, according to Zillow and Bankrate, just off last week's one year high.

ANDREW: So, a lot happened while most of us were off for the weekend. The headline is that Washington and Tehran are digging in ahead of Thursday's summit, the president took a direct shot at the Supreme Court, and in tech, Google made an unusually candid disclosure about its own AI. Let's start with the White House and the courts.

ANDREW: Over the weekend, President Trump used social media to call the Supreme Court's rulings this year, quote, faulty, political and ridiculous, end quote, and said they've cost the country trillions of dollars.

JENNY: Which rulings is he talking about?

ANDREW: Two big ones. Back in February, the Court ruled that the emergency powers law he used to impose his twenty twenty five tariffs didn't actually authorize them. Then in June, the Court upheld birthright citizenship under the fourteenth amendment, rejecting his executive order trying to end it. Both were setbacks for the administration, and he's clearly still frustrated by them.

JENNY: Did anyone push back on that over the weekend?

ANDREW: Democrats did, though from a different angle. One senator renewed a call for Supreme Court term limits and tighter ethics rules. And former Vice President Kamala Harris said this weekend she'd support expanding the Court to thirteen seats. Neither of those has any real path forward with this Congress, but it tells you the fight over the Court's legitimacy is becoming a bigger part of the political conversation, not a smaller one.

JENNY: How unusual is it for a sitting president to go after the Court this directly?

ANDREW: It's not unprecedented. Franklin Roosevelt famously tried to pack the Court in the nineteen thirties after a string of rulings against his New Deal programs. But the personal, public nature of these attacks, aimed at named justices rather than just the institution, is unusual for modern presidents, even ones who've disagreed sharply with the Court before.

ANDREW: Now, to the more urgent story. Iran's position on the Strait of Hormuz just got harder, not softer, heading into Thursday.

JENNY: Harder how?

ANDREW: Iran's parliament speaker said Sunday that Tehran won't reopen the strait or return to negotiations in their previous format until Washington meets Iran's conditions first. That's a firmer line than we'd heard even a week ago. Meanwhile, US Central Command says it's redirected roughly a hundred nine commercial vessels to enforce its blockade on Iranian ports, and shipping through the strait itself remains far below normal, only a handful of vessels transiting last Thursday against a ten day average more than three times that.

JENNY: And this is all happening right as Trump and Xi are set to meet.

ANDREW: Exactly. China has been positioning itself as the go-between, pushing both Washington and Tehran to rebuild some kind of negotiating channel. Thursday's summit in Washington gives Xi a direct chance to raise it face to face with Trump. Nothing suggests a breakthrough is close, but it's the most concrete opportunity either side has had in weeks.

JENNY: What's all of this doing to oil prices?

ANDREW: Keeping them elevated. Crude has been trading above a hundred dollars a barrel, and roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply normally moves through that strait. As long as shipping stays suppressed like this, that's a floor under prices, not a ceiling, and it's one more thing feeding into the inflation picture the Fed is watching.

ANDREW: One more national item worth a quick update. The fight between the White House and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh hasn't escalated further over the weekend, but it hasn't cooled off either. Warsh, who the Senate confirmed back in May, led a unanimous Fed vote on September sixteenth to raise rates a quarter point, the first hike in three years, over the president's public objections. Trump says he still has, quote, confidence in Warsh, but keeps calling the rest of the board hostile. Worth watching whether that unanimous vote holds the next time the Fed meets.

JENNY: Did bond markets react to any of that over the weekend?

ANDREW: Not directly, bond trading was closed Saturday and Sunday, so Friday's close is the level heading into today. But the ten-year breaking above five percent for the first time since 2007 happened in that same stretch of Fed tension, and it's worth watching whether that yield keeps climbing once trading resumes this morning.

ANDREW: Jenny, speaking of the Fed, all of this is landing directly on mortgage rates.

JENNY: Andrew, what's happening on the home lending side?

ANDREW: Rates are sitting near a one year high, though they've eased just slightly from last week's peak. Freddie Mac's weekly survey, published Thursday, put the thirty year fixed at six point nine five percent, up from six point seven six the week before, and the highest reading since January of twenty twenty five. Mortgage News Daily's daily tracker, which moves faster, hit seven point two percent by Thursday after peaking at seven point two four midweek. This morning, both Zillow and Bankrate's Optimal Blue index have it closer to seven percent, so there's been a modest pullback, but we're still well above where rates sat a month ago.

JENNY: So what does that actually mean for somebody trying to buy right now?

ANDREW: It means affordability keeps getting squeezed even though home prices themselves haven't moved much. The Mortgage Bankers Association's last weekly read, for the week ending September eleventh, showed loan applications down four point one percent, and adjustable rate mortgages taking a bigger share of the market than they have since June, which is usually a sign buyers are hunting for any way to lower a monthly payment. The next weekly application data, covering last week, is due Wednesday, and it'll be our first real look at whether this run-up in rates is pushing buyers to the sidelines entirely.

ANDREW: On the regulatory side, it was a quiet weekend, no fresh moves from the CFPB or FHFA to flag.

JENNY: We'll be watching that Wednesday number. Speaking of things moving fast, let's turn to AI, because Google had a pretty remarkable admission this weekend.

JENNY: Google disclosed on Thursday that during a security test back in May, its Gemini AI agents actually broke into three real companies, not simulated targets.

ANDREW: Wait, real companies? How did that happen?

JENNY: A test environment got misconfigured with live internet access instead of being sealed off. The Gemini agents, which were supposed to be practicing offensive security techniques in a sandbox, ended up breaching three outside systems for real, once by guessing a password and twice using credentials they found sitting in a public code repository. According to the reporting, the agents actually stopped themselves once they realized they'd broken into systems that were real, not test targets.

ANDREW: That's remarkable on two levels, honestly. The mistake, and the fact the AI recognized it.

JENNY: It is. And it lands right as banks and other financial firms are racing to deploy their own AI agents for things like fraud detection and back office work. If a major lab's own internal test can go this sideways, it's a pretty direct signal to any enterprise buyer to slow down and scrutinize how their vendors are sandboxing these systems before turning them loose.

JENNY: Right, and Google sat on that disclosure for about seven weeks before going public with it last week. It's a useful reminder that as these companies build more autonomous, agentic AI systems, the guardrails around testing them are just as important as the guardrails around deploying them.

JENNY: Separately, ahead of Thursday's summit, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrapped up talks with China's Vice Premier He Lifeng in New York on Sunday. CNN reported the US proposed a new notification system so both countries flag AI incidents that touch national security before they escalate into bigger disputes.

ANDREW: That's a notable idea given how much friction there already is between the two countries on trade and technology.

JENNY: There's also a real development in the industry safety conversation we've been following since Anthropic's Dario Amodei published his essay calling for a deliberate slowdown in the AI race. No multi-lab agreement has emerged, but Anthropic and the consulting firm Accenture are reportedly planning to invest roughly a billion dollars each over five years to embed independent evaluators directly inside Anthropic's operations. Sam Altman says OpenAI intends to match that kind of embedded-evaluator commitment. It's not a binding industry-wide pact, more like companies moving in parallel, but it's a step past just talk. Protests calling for a formal slowdown continued in San Francisco and Washington over the weekend.

JENNY: Andrew, let's bring it home to Jacksonville.

JENNY: Weather-wise, Jacksonville is looking at a high near eighty seven today, with a mix of sun and clouds, a chance of showers before sunrise and again this afternoon, and a moderate rip current risk if you're headed to the beach. Cooler, more fall-like air moves in later this week once the equinox hits tomorrow.

JENNY: The city council's budget fight over affordable housing money is still headed for a decision tomorrow, Tuesday. As we've reported, the Finance Committee voted seven to one last week to strip four point nine million dollars that Mayor Deegan had proposed for the affordable housing trust fund, with Council President Nick Howland casting the deciding vote. Councilman Matt Carlucci is planning to offer a floor amendment tomorrow to restore that money, split between new construction, down payment assistance, and utility hookup costs for low income residents.

ANDREW: Does he have the votes for that?

JENNY: It's not clear yet. The council auditor says restoring the funding needs a majority of members actually present at tomorrow's meeting, so attendance is going to matter as much as the arguments themselves. We'll know by tomorrow evening whether that four point nine million dollars gets restored.

JENNY: Two other local stories to track this week. JEA still hasn't set a timeline for finding a permanent CEO. Vickie Cavey's resignation takes effect Thursday, interim CEO Jody Brooks stays in the role, and the utility's board doesn't meet again until September twenty ninth, so a formal search process is still pending even as JEA presses ahead with roughly six hundred ninety million dollars in infrastructure work already underway.

JENNY: And JTA's board is still weighing six different options for the aging Skyway system downtown, ranging from about a hundred fifty two million dollars to modernize it up to five hundred sixty five million for a full streetcar conversion. A preferred option isn't expected until sometime in October.

JENNY: On a brighter note downtown, the Vandeveer building in the Pearl Square district of Gateway Jax is welcoming its first residents this month, part of that roughly one billion dollar redevelopment project, with new restaurants and retail opening at street level.

ANDREW: Good to see something downtown actually opening its doors instead of just being planned.

ANDREW: And I'll guess Sunday wasn't a great day for Jaguars fans either.

JENNY: No, it wasn't. Trevor Lawrence and the offense couldn't hold onto a second half lead in Denver, and Jacksonville dropped that one twenty to thirteen. The Jaguars head back home to Duval County at .500, looking to regroup before next week's matchup.

ANDREW: Before we let you go, one thing to watch this week: Thursday's summit in Washington between President Trump and China's Xi Jinping. Iran's Strait of Hormuz standoff and the broader tariff relationship between the two countries are both expected to be on the table. Watch for whether China uses its leverage to actually extract any movement from either Washington or Tehran on reopening shipping through the strait, because right now, both sides are further apart than they were a week ago, not closer. A concrete step toward reopening that shipping lane would be the clearest sign the summit actually produced something, rather than just another round of talks.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Monday. Have a great start to your week.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Mortgage Rates Hit 20-Month High as Markets Rebound, AI Labs Talk Safety
item.description: Freddie Mac confirms mortgage rates at their highest since January 2025 as Wall Street claws back the Fed-hike selloff. Plus, rival AI labs open safety talks, and Jacksonville's housing budget fight heads to a final vote.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Friday, September 18th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: Freddie Mac made it official overnight. The average thirty-year mortgage rate has hit its highest level in twenty months, a direct hangover from Wednesday's Fed hike. We'll get into what that means for anyone house-hunting this fall.

ANDREW: And in tech, Anthropic's CEO published an essay last week arguing the industry should deliberately slow down, and it's reportedly kicked off real safety talks between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind. We'll get into why three rivals are suddenly comparing notes.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,637, up about 1.1 percent. The Dow gained 316 points, roughly six tenths of a percent, to close at 51,778. The Nasdaq jumped roughly 1.7 percent to about 26,418. It was a sharp reversal. Stocks clawed back nearly all of Wednesday's post-Fed selloff as Treasury yields and oil prices eased. The ten-year Treasury yield pulled back to around 4.9 percent, down from the 5 percent-plus level it touched on Fed day. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at 7.19 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, actually down slightly from Wednesday's spike.

ANDREW: Let's start with what that mortgage number really means, because there's a more official read out this morning that tells a clearer story. Freddie Mac's weekly rate survey came out at noon yesterday, and it put the average thirty-year fixed at 6.95 percent, up from 6.76 percent the week before. That's the highest reading in that survey since January of last year.

JENNY: So the Mortgage News Daily number and the Freddie Mac number are actually moving in different directions right now?

ANDREW: Right, and that's just a quirk of methodology. Mortgage News Daily tracks live daily quotes for the sharpest borrowers, while Freddie Mac surveys lenders once a week and captures a broader average, so it lags. But the direction over the last two weeks is the same story. Rates jumped fast after the Fed's hike, and even with the daily tracker easing off its Wednesday peak, Freddie Mac's slower-moving number is only now catching up to just how much ground was lost. For somebody shopping for a loan today, 6.95 percent is the number that reflects what a typical lender is actually quoting.

JENNY: What does that do to someone's monthly payment compared to a month ago?

ANDREW: On a typical 400,000 dollar loan, moving from the high sixes to just under 7 percent adds somewhere around 150 to 200 dollars a month. It's not catastrophic, but it's enough to price some buyers out or push them toward an adjustable-rate loan, which is exactly what we saw in this week's Mortgage Bankers Association data. ARM share is now at its highest point since June.

ANDREW: Beyond the rate itself, it was a quiet stretch for mortgage regulation, no new moves from the CFPB or FHFA to flag today. The next real data point is the Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly application survey, due out around the 23rd or 24th, which will show whether this rate jump has actually pushed buyers to the sidelines.

ANDREW: Zoom out to Washington, and the whipsaw this week has been remarkable. Stocks fell hard Wednesday when the Fed hiked, then nearly fully recovered by Thursday's close as yields eased. Through it all, President Trump kept up the pressure on his own pick for Fed chair. He told reporters again that he wants rates at 1 percent or lower, and repeated that he'd told Kevin Warsh directly to, quote, vote with the board because it's not going to matter.

JENNY: Didn't Warsh vote with the board anyway, unanimously?

ANDREW: He did, and that's still the notable thread here. Two days after a hike the president publicly opposed, market volatility has settled down without the Fed visibly bending. Whether that holds through the next meeting under continued pressure is the real question, but so far the numbers suggest markets are more rattled by the uncertainty of a Trump-Fed standoff than by the actual quarter-point move itself. It also suggests investors read Thursday's rally as a vote of confidence in the Fed's independence, not just relief that the hike is behind them.

ANDREW: The other story we're still tracking runs through Beijing. China's foreign minister, Wang Yi, met again with Iran's Araghchi this week, pushing both Tehran and Washington toward what he called substantive consultations, and pressing for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen fully. Shipping through the strait actually ticked down. Only four vessels transited on Tuesday, down from seven the day before, still well short of normal traffic. Iran continues to rule out direct talks with the US, though it hasn't shut the door on something indirect. With the Trump-Xi summit six days out, that's the thread to watch.

JENNY: Any sign Beijing's actually making headway, or is this still just talk?

ANDREW: Still just talk for now. Until shipping volumes recover or Tehran shifts its public position, this stays a background story rather than a resolution.

ANDREW: Jenny, from Beijing to Silicon Valley, you've got a genuinely unusual story brewing in AI this morning.

JENNY: I do. It traces back to an essay Anthropic's CEO, Dario Amodei, published last week, arguing the entire industry should deliberately slow down how fast these models get more capable, by a year or two, specifically to give safety research time to catch up. Anthropic also committed on its own to giving outside evaluators permanent, employee-level access to its models, which is a level of outside scrutiny frontier labs don't typically offer.

ANDREW: That seems like a strange thing for a company racing to build the best AI to volunteer.

JENNY: It is, but it's landed. TechCrunch is reporting the essay kicked off real safety talks over the past couple of weeks between OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google DeepMind, three companies that are normally fighting over the same customers and engineers. Sam Altman and even Elon Musk both publicly praised the essay, which is notable given how often those two clash with Anthropic.

JENNY: It's also drawn a response out on the street. Protesters marched from OpenAI's San Francisco offices to Anthropic's yesterday and today, demanding the labs actually slow the race down, not just talk about it.

ANDREW: Is there any indication this turns into something concrete, or is it still just conversation?

JENNY: Still conversation for now, and that's worth being honest about. The Trump administration is pushing labs the other direction, toward prioritizing competitiveness with China over any safety slowdown. So there's real tension between what these three companies are discussing privately and the political pressure they're under publicly.

JENNY: On the product side, both of the moves we flagged earlier this week are now rolling out for real. OpenAI's sponsored agents, those interactive ad conversations inside ChatGPT, are expanding beyond the US starting next week with a new Shopify ads integration. And Anthropic's merged Claude and Cowork interface, plus its new Docs and Slides tools, are live in beta for Pro and Max subscribers, with enterprise customers getting thirty days notice before anything changes for them.

JENNY: One quick legal update, too. Remember the settlement Elon Musk's companies reached with Apple that a judge wanted to see? He reviewed it privately, and ruled it isn't actually relevant to the ongoing case against OpenAI, which continues as the sole remaining defendant. The terms themselves are staying confidential.

ANDREW: So all that drama over the settlement, and it turned out to be a non-event.

JENNY: Pretty much, at least for now.

JENNY: Let's bring it home to Jacksonville. Weather-wise, we're looking at a high near 89 degrees today, mostly sunny and breezy, with northeast winds up to 16 miles an hour and gusts as high as 24. Lows tonight near 75, with no rain expected.

JENNY: The big one to watch locally is a budget fight at city hall. City council takes its final vote on the roughly two-billion-dollar city budget this coming Tuesday, September 22nd, and Councilman Matt Carlucci is pushing to restore 4.9 million dollars that the Finance Committee voted to strip from the affordable housing trust fund, a seven-to-one vote where Council President Nick Howland cast the deciding vote to cut it.

ANDREW: What's actually riding on that 4.9 million?

JENNY: It breaks into three pieces. About 2.4 million for building new affordable units, 1.5 million for down-payment assistance for workforce buyers, and 1 million to cover utility tap-in costs. Carlucci says he's not trying to dictate how it's spent, just trying to make sure the money is there. To restore it, he needs a majority of whoever's on the council floor Tuesday, at least ten votes if all nineteen members show up.

ANDREW: That's a real fight over a small slice of a two-billion-dollar budget.

JENNY: It is, but advocates say it's the piece that actually helps first-time buyers get into a home, which is why it's become the thing to watch heading into Tuesday.

JENNY: Over at JEA, the leadership transition keeps moving even as the utility pushes ahead on major projects. CEO Vickie Cavey's resignation still takes effect next Friday, September 25th, with interim CEO Jody Brooks running things day to day. JEA says it's moving forward on roughly 690 million dollars in water infrastructure work, including a more than 220 million dollar expansion in northwest St. Johns County and a nearly 193 million dollar facility near the airport. The board still hasn't announced a timeline for a permanent CEO search.

JENNY: And JTA is still working through what to do about the downtown Skyway. The agency has confirmed the cost range for its six options at just under 152 million dollars on the low end up to about 565 million on the high end. That top option, a modern streetcar system, would also add nearly 16 million dollars a year in upkeep. JTA's interim CEO says everything is still on the table, including the city's existing 247 million dollar gas-tax funding agreement, and no decision date has been set.

ANDREW: Six options and no front-runner yet, that's a lot still up in the air for a system that's already near the end of its life.

JENNY: It is, and JTA keeps saying it wants more public input before narrowing anything down, which is part of why this keeps stretching out.

JENNY: Two more worth a quick mention. The Jaguars' one point four billion dollar stadium overhaul is still rising on schedule for an August 2028 finish, with the team playing a reduced-capacity season downtown in the meantime. And a new twenty-million-dollar housing fund backed by Northern Trust and the Jessie Ball duPont Fund already has two deals in the pipeline that together could unlock more than 300 affordable units.

ANDREW: That's a nice complement to the fight over that 4.9 million at city hall.

JENNY: It is, private money moving on affordable housing while the public side is still arguing over its piece of the budget.

JENNY: Andrew, before we let everyone go?

ANDREW: One thing to watch: Tuesday's city council budget vote here in Jacksonville, and whether Carlucci's amendment restores that affordable housing money. But nationally, keep an eye on next week's Mortgage Bankers Association data, due out around the 23rd or 24th. It'll be the first real look at whether this rate spike above 6.9 percent has actually pushed buyers off the sidelines, or whether the market shrugs it off heading into the fall selling season. Either answer tells us something about how much staying power this Fed-driven rate jump really has.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Friday. Have a great weekend.

ANDREW: We'll see you Monday.

item.title: Jax Morning Brief — Fed Hikes Rates as Warsh Bucks Trump, Mortgages Top 7 Percent
item.description: The Fed's first rate hike since 2023 sends mortgage rates above 7 percent and Treasury yields past 5. Plus, Iran diplomacy in Beijing, Anthropic folds Cowork into Claude, and Jacksonville's JEA presses ahead on 690 million dollars in projects.
item.content:encoded:
Good morning. It's Thursday, September 17th. This is The Morning Brief. I'm Jenny.

ANDREW: And I'm Andrew.

JENNY: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates yesterday for the first time since 2023, and Wall Street did not like it. We'll get into why Chair Kevin Warsh pushed the hike through over the president's very public objections, and what it's already doing to mortgage rates.

ANDREW: And in tech, Anthropic just tore down the wall between its Claude chatbot and its Cowork product, folding them into a single interface. We'll get into what that means for how people actually use these tools day to day.

JENNY: Let's get into it.

ANDREW: A quick look at the markets. The S and P 500 closed at 7,551, down about half a percent. The Dow lost 631 points, a drop of roughly 1.2 percent, to close at 51,462. The Nasdaq was essentially flat, down just a hair, which is a little surprising given how sensitive tech stocks usually are to higher rates. It was a rough afternoon for stocks as investors digested a Fed that sounded more hawkish than expected. The ten-year Treasury yield pushed back above 5 percent, a level it hadn't touched since before the 2008 financial crisis. And the thirty-year fixed mortgage rate is tracking at roughly 7.24 percent according to Mortgage News Daily, the highest it's been since January of last year.

ANDREW: Let's start with what's driving all of this, because the mortgage number is really the headline for anyone thinking about buying or refinancing right now. Mortgage News Daily says the top-tier thirty-year fixed has climbed for six straight days, up about a third of a point in less than a week. That's the sharpest jump they've tracked since October of last year.

JENNY: How does that compare to where things stood even a month ago?

ANDREW: A month ago, borrowers were looking at rates closer to 6.7, 6.8 percent. So this is a genuinely fast move, not a gradual drift. And it's showing up immediately in the data. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest weekly survey, covering the week ending September 11th, showed total applications down four percent, refinances down nine percent, and purchase applications down slightly too. More borrowers are shifting into adjustable-rate loans just to soften the blow — the ARM share is now at its highest level since June.

JENNY: So somebody who was pre-approved a few weeks ago might come back to a very different number.

ANDREW: Exactly right, and that's the real-world sting here. A quarter point or half point on a mortgage rate can mean hundreds of dollars a month on a typical loan. One wrinkle worth flagging: Freddie Mac's official weekly rate survey still shows thirty-year rates at 6.76 percent, because that reading predates this week's spike. That number updates today, and it's going to have some catching up to do.

ANDREW: That mortgage spike traces directly back to what happened in Washington yesterday afternoon. The Fed's rate-setting committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark rate by a quarter point, to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent. It's the first hike since 2023, and the first of Kevin Warsh's tenure as chair. In his press conference, Warsh said inflation has been, quote, too high for too long, and pointed to a strengthening economy, stalled progress on inflation, and rising geopolitical tension as the reasons the Fed couldn't wait any longer. The committee's new projections pencil in one more hike before year's end, but nothing further in 2027.

JENNY: Trump handpicked Warsh for this job. How did the White House take a rate hike?

ANDREW: About as well as you'd expect. Trump told reporters he wants rates at 1 percent or lower, and said he'd told Warsh directly, quote, you might as well vote with the board, because it's not going to matter. He kept saying he still has confidence in Warsh personally, but called the rest of the Fed's board hostile. The notable thing is that the vote was unanimous anyway — for now, that suggests the Fed's independence is holding even under direct pressure from the president, which wasn't a given heading into this meeting.

JENNY: Is there any risk that pressure campaign works eventually?

ANDREW: It's the thing to watch over the next few meetings. One hike doesn't settle that question, but a unanimous vote right after very public pressure is at least a data point in the Fed's favor. Historically, Fed chairs who've faced this kind of direct presidential lobbying have tended to lean harder into their independence, not less, at least in the meeting right after the pressure goes public. Whether that holds for Warsh past this one decision is a different question.

ANDREW: The other story we're watching out of Washington runs through Beijing. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, met with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi there yesterday, and China publicly urged both Iran and the US to return to talks and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. It's a notable back-channel move a week ahead of the planned Trump-Xi summit on September 24th.

JENNY: Is that actually a sign the standoff is easing, or just talk?

ANDREW: Still too early to call it a breakthrough. Tehran's Supreme National Security Council has publicly rejected direct talks with Washington until the US ends military operations and lifts sanctions. But shipping traffic through the Strait did pick up somewhat — twelve vessels transited on Tuesday, double the day before, though still well short of pre-war norms, and Brent crude remains elevated in the high hundred-and-single-digits per barrel. With the Trump-Xi summit coming up fast, Beijing inserting itself into the Iran conversation is worth watching closely.

ANDREW: Jenny, from Washington and Beijing to something a lot closer to your beat — what's happening in AI this morning?

JENNY: Anthropic made a pretty significant product change yesterday. They merged their Claude chatbot and their Cowork tool, which had been separate products, into one single interface. There's no more picking a mode — you just describe what you need, and Claude decides whether that's a quick answer or a bigger project. They're also rolling out new Claude Docs and Claude Slides tools in beta, including the ability to export a presentation straight to PowerPoint or PDF.

ANDREW: Why split them up in the first place if they were just going to merge them back?

JENNY: According to Anthropic, users kept saying the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged, because work you started in the chat didn't carry over into Cowork, and vice versa. So now it's just one product that routes automatically. It's rolling out to Pro and Max subscribers first, on web, desktop, and mobile, with free and team tiers to follow later.

JENNY: Meanwhile, OpenAI is testing something it's calling Sponsored Agents inside ChatGPT. When a sponsored ad shows up in a conversation, users can opt into a separate, clearly labeled chat with a business's AI agent — ask it questions, get details, and click through to buy. OpenAI also rolled out new tools letting advertisers build and manage those ChatGPT ad campaigns directly from HubSpot and Shopify, its first CRM and ecommerce partners for the ad product.

ANDREW: So conversational advertising, built right into the chatbot itself.

JENNY: Exactly. It's clearly separated from ChatGPT's own answers, but it's another sign these AI platforms are building out real advertising businesses, not just relying on subscriptions.

JENNY: One more from the legal side worth a quick mention. A federal judge is pressing Elon Musk's companies, X and xAI, to hand over the terms of a settlement they quietly reached with Apple this month. The two had sued Apple and OpenAI together, alleging an exclusive deal made ChatGPT the only chatbot built into the iPhone. X and xAI dropped their claims against Apple specifically, but the judge wants to see what was actually agreed to before letting them walk away — and their case against OpenAI itself continues.

ANDREW: Interesting that Musk's own companies are the ones facing the judge's skepticism there.

JENNY: Right, it's a reminder that a lot of the AI industry's biggest rivalries are also tangled up in the same courtrooms.

JENNY: Let's bring it home to Jacksonville. Weather-wise, we're looking at a high near 87 degrees today, mostly sunny and breezy, with northeast winds gusting up to 24 miles an hour. Rain chances stay low, around 20 percent.

JENNY: The big local story is JEA. The utility confirmed this week it's moving ahead with roughly 690 million dollars in infrastructure projects even as its leadership is in flux. That includes a more than 220 million dollar water expansion in northwest St. Johns County, a nearly 193 million dollar facility near Jacksonville International Airport, and a project in East Arlington costing just under 165 million that also adds high-level disinfection. This comes as CEO Vickie Cavey's resignation takes effect on September 25th, with interim CEO Jody Brooks currently running day-to-day operations.

ANDREW: Any word on who might actually replace her, or is the board still figuring that out?

JENNY: Still figuring it out. JEA hasn't set a public timeline yet for a permanent search — the board says operations and strategy won't change in the meantime, but that leadership question is very much unresolved heading into next week, and it's worth remembering this utility has already had a rocky year of governance headlines.

JENNY: Speaking of next week, city council is heading toward a final vote on Jacksonville's roughly two-billion-dollar budget on Tuesday, September 22nd. Councilman Matt Carlucci is pushing an amendment to restore 4.9 million dollars that the Finance Committee voted, seven to one, to strip from the city's affordable housing trust fund. That money would split three ways — about 2.4 million for new construction, 1.5 million for down-payment assistance, and 1 million for utility tap-in costs.

ANDREW: That's a pretty specific fight over a pretty small slice of a two-billion-dollar budget.

JENNY: It is, but advocates say it's the piece that actually helps first-time and workforce buyers get into a home, which is exactly why Carlucci is making a public push to get it back in before Tuesday's vote. He's said he's not trying to dictate how the money gets spent, just that it needs to be there.

JENNY: One more to flag: JTA is still working through what to do with the downtown Skyway, which is nearing the end of its usable life. There are six alternatives on the table now, ranging from about 152 million dollars to 565 million, everything from converting it into an elevated trail to building a modern streetcar to folding it into JTA's autonomous-vehicle program. An earlier round of public input drew about 12,000 comments, which is actually what pushed a cable-car option onto the list that wasn't there originally. Another round of public meetings is continuing through this month before JTA narrows things down.

ANDREW: It's rare for a transit agency to actually add an option because of public feedback instead of trimming the list.

JENNY: It is, and it's part of why this process has dragged on as long as it has — JTA keeps saying it wants to hear from residents before locking anything in.

JENNY: Andrew, before we let everyone go?

ANDREW: One thing to watch today: Freddie Mac publishes its official weekly mortgage rate survey at noon Eastern. Last week's reading was 6.76 percent, which is already stale given this week's run-up on the daily trackers toward 7.24 percent. Watch how much of that gap closes. If Freddie Mac's number jumps most of the way there, it confirms buyers are now facing the highest widely-reported mortgage rates in over a year, right as the fall home-buying season kicks in and just one week ahead of that Trump-Xi summit that could move markets all over again.

JENNY: That's your Morning Brief for Thursday. Have a great day.

ANDREW: We'll see you tomorrow.
